issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may reject a challenge to a Board’s monetary jurisdiction when the challenge was not raised at trial and doing so deprived the opposing party of an opportunity to establish that the Board had the necessary sanction.
material_facts: The challenge to the Board’s jurisdiction based on the amount of the debt was first raised on appeal, not in the trial court.
The governing framework allowed the Board to deal with debts above the ordinary threshold if it had the Collector’s prior written sanction.
Had the issue been raised at trial, the respondents could have had the opportunity to show that the sanction had been obtained.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the jurisdictional objection because it had not been raised at trial and the respondents had therefore lacked an opportunity to establish that the Board had the required sanction; the Court did not decide whether the debt exceeded the ordinary threshold.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 144 framed under the Bengal Agricultural Debtors Act set an ordinary maximum for debts dealt with by a Board, but its proviso permitted the Board, with the Collector’s prior written sanction, to deal with a higher amount. Because the objection was not raised at trial, the respondents had no opportunity to show that the sanction had been obtained, and the Court declined to determine the actual debt amount. No earlier cases are relied on.

rule.if: board_jurisdiction_challenge_in_appeal and objection_not_raised_at_trial and sanction_could_authorize_higher_debt and opposing_party_lost_opportunity_to_prove_sanction

predicates.board_jurisdiction_challenge_in_appeal: A party in an appeal from a civil proceeding challenges a Board’s authority to deal with the matter because the debt exceeds the ordinary monetary threshold.
predicates.objection_not_raised_at_trial: The party did not raise the jurisdictional objection in the trial court.
predicates.sanction_could_authorize_higher_debt: The governing framework allowed the Board to deal with a higher debt if the required prior sanction had been obtained.
predicates.opposing_party_lost_opportunity_to_prove: Because the objection was not raised at trial, the opposing party did not have an opportunity there to establish that the sanction had been obtained.
predicates.appellate_court_rejects_late_jurisdictio: The appellate court rejects the jurisdictional objection without deciding the disputed debt amount.

issues.definition: When a party first challenges a Board’s monetary authority on appeal, and the opposing party thereby lost the opportunity to prove that sanction permitted the higher amount, the appellate court rejects the late objection.

issues.legal_issue: After an execution sale is set aside in an eligible agricultural-debtor restoration proceeding, a subsequent transferee who possesses the property is subject to ejectment unless the transfer or possession falls within a stated exception.
material_facts: The debtor’s property was sold in execution of a mortgage decree, and the decree-holder purchased it.
After the statutory restoration procedure was introduced, the debtors applied to the Board and obtained an award entitling them to restoration.
The decree-holder transferred the property to the appellant after the relevant cutoff date.
The debtors obtained possession following the Board proceedings, but the appellant later disturbed their possession.
The appellant claimed that she was a bona fide purchaser for value from the decree-holder, not an under-raiyat of the debtor.
issues.conclusion: The appellant, as a transferee from the decree-holder, was covered by the statutory restoration provision and could be ejected after the sale was set aside; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 37-A(1)(c) and 37-A(8) of the Bengal Agricultural Debtors Act must be read together. Section 37-A(8) directs that the sale be set aside and that any person in possession be ejected, subject to the specified under-raiyat exception. Its words “any person” include a subsequent transferee whose right to possession derives from the sale. Section 37-A(1)(c) preserves only specified kinds of bona fide alienations made before the cutoff date; a later bona fide transfer for value is not excluded. The inclusive definition of “decree-holder” in section 37-A(12) also supports the broad reading. No earlier cases are relied on.

rule.if: agricultural_debtor_restoration_proceeding and eligible_restoration_award_made and execution_sale_set_aside and person_possesses_through_sale and not protected_under_raiyat_possession and not transfer_within_preserved_class

predicates.agricultural_debtor_restoration_proceedi: The proceeding seeks restoration of property sold in execution on behalf of an agricultural debtor.
predicates.eligible_restoration_award_made: The debtor obtained an award under the restoration procedure after satisfying its eligibility conditions.
predicates.execution_sale_set_aside: The sale of the property in execution is set aside pursuant to the restoration award.
predicates.person_possesses_through_sale: A person other than the debtor possesses the property by virtue of the execution sale or a later transfer deriving from that sale.
predicates.protected_under_raiyat_possession: The person possesses the property as an under-raiyat of the debtor under the circumstances protected by the restoration provision.
predicates.transfer_within_preserved_class: The decree-holder made the transfer before the applicable cutoff, and the transfer belongs to one of the specified preserved categories.
predicates.nonexempt_possessor_is_ejected: A person possessing the property through the sale is subject to ejectment, unless an applicable possession or transfer exception protects that person.

issues.definition: When an eligible debtor obtains a restoration award, the execution sale is set aside, and a person possesses the property through that sale, the person is subject to ejectment unless the stated possession or transfer exception applies.
